faq.a: PCV can be measured with a simple centrifuge and visual readout, requiring no electricity or reagents, whereas haemoglobin often needs a calibrated analyser.
faq.q: Why is PCV preferred over haemoglobin in some low‑resource settings?

faq.a: Yes; early iron deficiency may not lower PCV yet; ferritin or transferrin saturation is needed for confirmation.
faq.q: Can a child have a normal PCV but still be iron deficient?

faq.a: Isotonic oral rehydration solution or normal saline; avoid hypotonic fluids that could worsen hyponatraemia.
faq.q: What is the safest fluid for correcting dehydration‑related high PCV?

exam: A 3‑year‑old with fever, pallor and a PCV of 12 % – what are the next three investigations and why? — Peripheral smear for malaria, rapid malaria test, and serum ferritin; they identify malaria‑related haemolysis or iron deficiency.

A child presents with a sunken fontanelle, PCV 48 % and urine output <1 mL/kg/h – what is your immediate management? — Give ORS bolus 20 mL/kg, reassess PCV after rehydration; avoid unnecessary transfusion.

How does sickle‑cell disease cause a low PCV and what specific treatment would you start? — Chronic haemolysis lowers PCV; start folic acid and penicillin prophylaxis, arrange vaccination, and plan transfusion if PCV <15 %.

A patient with severe malaria has PCV 18 % and signs of shock – what are the key steps before transfusion? — Stabilise airway, give IV crystalloid bolus, start antimalarial therapy, cross‑match blood; monitor for fluid overload.

Why is iron supplementation contraindicated in a child with PCV 22 % and a positive malaria test? — Iron can fuel parasite growth and increase oxidative stress; treat malaria first, then reassess iron need.

What clinical sign differentiates dehydration‑related high PCV from true polycythaemia? — Sunken fontanelle and dry mucous membranes point to dehydration, whereas a ruddy complexion without dehydration signs suggests polycythaemia.
Explain why a recent acute bleed may show a normal PCV on presentation. — Plasma shifts into the vascular space within minutes, temporarily maintaining PCV despite red cell loss.
When is exchange transfusion indicated for a child with high PCV? — In severe hyperviscosity with neurological symptoms (headache, seizures) where PCV ≥55 % and fluid therapy fails.
ai.title: Packed Cell Volume in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Packed cell volume (PCV) is the proportion of whole blood occupied by red cells. It is a rapid bedside estimate of haemoglobin and guides diagnosis of anaemia, dehydration and polycythaemia in low‑resource settings.

b: Normal range in children 1‑5 years: 30‑40 % (varies with age and altitude).
A bedside capillary PCV can be read with a simple micro‑haematocrit reader when a full laboratory is unavailable.
sections.p: PCV is measured by centrifuging a micro‑capillary tube of whole blood; the red cell column is read as a percentage of total column length.

t.b: Provides a quantitative PCV; values <30 % suggest anaemia, >55 % suggest polycythaemia.

t.a: Clinical assessment (skin pallor, fontanelle status, capillary refill)
t.b: Correlates with PCV when lab is not available; a sunken fontanelle and delayed capillary refill point to dehydration‑related PCV rise.

b: Mild anaemia: PCV 25‑29 %
Moderate anaemia: PCV 15‑24 %
Severe anaemia: PCV <15 % (or Hb <5 g/dL).
Mild polycythaemia: PCV 41‑49 %
Severe polycythaemia: PCV ≥55 %.
sections.p: PCV guides severity grading of anaemia and polycythaemia, which informs urgency of treatment.

b: Anaemia: malaria, sickle‑cell disease, iron deficiency, hookworm, HIV‑related marrow suppression, chronic diarrhoea.
Polycythaemia: chronic hypoxia (high altitude, cyanotic heart disease), dehydration, congenital erythrocytosis.
sections.p: In East African paediatrics the most common drivers of abnormal PCV are infections, nutritional deficits and haemolysis.

b: Severe anaemia may cause a systolic flow murmur and widened pulse pressure.
Polycythaemia can produce headache, irritability and a ruddy complexion.
sections.p: Children with low PCV often appear pale, fatigued, tachypnoeic and may have a rapid heart rate; dehydration‑related high PCV presents with a sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes and reduced urine output.

b: Full blood count (FBC) for MCV, reticulocyte count, platelets.
Peripheral smear for malaria parasites, sickle cells, schistocytes.
Serum ferritin or iron studies when iron deficiency is suspected (if lab available).
sections.p: PCV is part of a basic haematology panel; additional tests clarify aetiology.

t.b: Detects malaria parasites, sickle cells, and haemolysis; a positive smear confirms malaria‑related anaemia.
Answers whether malaria is present when microscopy is unavailable; a positive test supports malaria as cause of low PCV.
Elevated urea with high PCV suggests dehydration; normal urea with low PCV points to true anaemia.

b: PCV <15 % with tachycardia >180 bpm, altered consciousness, or respiratory distress → urgent transfusion.
PCV ≥55 % with headache, vomiting, or seizures → risk of hyperviscosity syndrome.
sections.p: Severe derangements of PCV can rapidly become life‑threatening.

b: Anaemia: give oral iron for iron deficiency; start antimalarial therapy for malaria; initiate penicillin prophylaxis and folic acid for sickle‑cell disease; treat hookworm with albendazole.
Severe anaemia: arrange compatible blood transfusion; use whole‑blood or packed red cells, avoiding rapid over‑transfusion.
Polycythaemia from dehydration: give oral rehydration solution (ORS) or IV isotonic fluids; monitor for fluid overload.
Avoid iron in patients with active infection or haemolysis without proven deficiency.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; then correct the PCV abnormality while monitoring for complications.

b: Re‑check PCV 48‑72 h after transfusion or after completing antimalarial course.
In sickle‑cell disease, schedule PCV every 3‑6 months and provide routine vaccinations.
Promote insecticide‑treated nets, deworming, and iron‑rich complementary foods to prevent anaemia.
sections.p: Regular PCV monitoring tracks response to therapy and detects relapse.

b: Low PCV ≠ low plasma volume; dehydration raises PCV while plasma volume falls.
High PCV ≠ increased total blood volume; it may reflect haemoconcentration rather than true polycythaemia.
sections.p: PCV is sometimes mistaken for plasma volume or total blood volume.

b: Severe dehydration can give a falsely normal PCV if the sample is diluted by IV fluids.
Recent blood loss may show a normal PCV early because plasma shifts into the vascular space.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anaemia (PCV <15 %) with shock, altered consciousness or respiratory failure
